title: Oblates
hookLine: laypeople who follow the spirit of the Rule in ordinary life

lines: A NURSE, A MECHANIC, A MOTHER.
cards: A nurse finishing a night shift. A retired mechanic. A mother of three who keeps a worn copy of the Rule in the glove compartment.
None of them lives in a monastery or wears a habit. But each belongs, in a real way, to one particular abbey, and tries to live by Benedict's Rule in a house with a mortgage and a washing machine.
The family of Benedict has a branch that doesn't live behind any wall at all. Today's word: oblate.

teach.b: Oblate means one who is offered. The word goes back to the Rule itself.

In chapter fifty-nine, Benedict describes parents who offer a son to the monastery: they wrap the boy's hand, with their written promise, in the cloth of the altar, and so give him to God. That custom ended long ago.

But the word stayed, and came to name something new: men and women outside the cloister, single or married, who offer their lives to God in the spirit of the Rule while staying exactly where they are.

Today an oblate attaches to one particular monastery, usually after a time of getting to know it. In a short ceremony they make an oblation: a promise to live by the spirit of the Rule as their life allows.

teach.h: A PROMISE, NOT A MONK'S VOWS.
teach.b: It's a promise, not the vows of a monk. They don't move in, or give up their homes or marriages.

What they take home is the shape of the life: some of the psalms and prayers the monks pray, morning or evening; a daily time of slow reading with Scripture; work done carefully, as if the tools were altar vessels; guests received as Christ.

And a link to their monastery, which prays for them and which they visit when they can. Stability, in a different way: tied to one house, carrying its rhythm into a kitchen, a classroom, a hospital ward.
The Rule was written for people behind walls.
Oblates show that it fits through a front door.

how: Benedictine oblates attach themselves to a particular monastery, make an oblation after a period of preparation, and try to live the spirit of the Rule at home through daily prayer, spiritual reading and work.

o: a novice monk in training who hasn't yet taken vows
a gift of money promised to a monastery each year
a layperson tied to a monastery, living its Rule at home

p: a promise, not a monk's vows

s: they live at home, single or married, and carry the Rule's rhythm into ordinary life.
an oblate is tied to one particular monastery
they make their oblation with one house, which prays for them and which they visit when they can.
oblates take the same vows as monks
they make an oblation, a promise to live the spirit of the Rule as their life allows.

games.q: you love the Rule but you have a job, a family and a mortgage. what does the oblate path offer?
o: move into the monastery and take vows.
make a promise with one monastery and live its rhythm at home.
read the Rule once and leave it on the shelf.
games.why: oblates stay where they are, tied to one house by a promise, and bring the psalms, reading, work and hospitality home.

practice: Let yourself wonder where the closest community of monks or nuns might be, a hill outside town, a city block, a farm road, and picture its bell ringing for prayer while you sit here. You and they share this hour.
If you pray, pray with them, wherever they are; if not, just keep the quiet alongside them.

wordCard.voice: Oblate. One who is offered: a layperson tied to a Benedictine monastery, living the spirit of the Rule in ordinary life. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: offered, the sense behind the English word oblate.

carryVoice: Your line: the rule at home. A promise, not a monk's vows, and still a real belonging. See you tomorrow.
